title: Food & Cooking Shorts · Episode 4
chapters: Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature
Why chillies burn: the science of heat

units.t: Food & Cooking Shorts. Episode four.
In this episode: Umami and the MSG story, Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature and Why chillies burn: the science of heat.
Part one. Umami and the MSG story.
A Japanese chemist tasting his soup discovered a fifth basic taste.
The seasoning he created went on to become one of the most misunderstood ingredients in the world.
A chemist and his soup.
In 1908 the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda was enjoying dashi, a broth made with kombu seaweed, when he wondered about its distinctive savoury taste.
It was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter, the four tastes scientists recognised then.
Working with large quantities of kombu, he isolated crystals of glutamic acid, an amino acid, and showed that its salts carried the taste.
He named the sensation umami, from a Japanese word for delicious, roughly 'savoury deliciousness'.
Ikeda then found a stable, easy-to-use seasoning based on it, monosodium glutamate, or MSG.
With a business partner, he launched it in Japan in 1909 as Ajinomoto.
Glutamate is everywhere.
MSG sounds industrial, but glutamate is one of nature's most common amino acids.
Our bodies make it, and breast milk contains it.
Usually it is locked inside proteins, where we cannot taste it.
When proteins break down through ripening, ageing, drying, cooking or fermenting, free glutamate is released.
That is why ripe tomatoes taste more savoury than green ones, and why parmesan, soy sauce, fish sauce, miso, mushrooms, anchovies and Vegemite are so rich in depth.
Other Japanese scientists later found inosinate in dried bonito and guanylate in dried shiitake.
Combined with glutamate, these nucleotides multiply umami rather than adding to it.
Japanese dashi pairs kombu with bonito.
Western cooks pair tomatoes or parmesan with meat.
A fifth taste confirmed.
For decades many Western scientists doubted that umami was a separate taste.
They argued it was a blend of other tastes, or an effect of smell.
The debate shifted in the early 2000s, when researchers identified taste receptors on the tongue that respond specifically to glutamate, giving umami a clear biological basis.
Today it is widely accepted as the fifth basic taste, alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
Why would we evolve to detect it?
A common explanation is that umami signals protein.
Glutamate is released when protein-rich foods are cooked or aged, so a taste that rewards it steers us towards nourishing food.
Sweetness signals energy from sugars, bitterness may warn of toxins, and sourness of unripe or spoiled food.
How a rumour began.
For its first half-century MSG drew few complaints.

In 1968 a doctor wrote to a prominent medical journal describing numbness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States, wondering whether cooking wine, sodium or MSG was to blame.
The term 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' spread through newspapers, and restaurants posted 'no MSG' signs.
Many now see the panic as tinged with prejudice, since parmesan, tomatoes and stock were rarely blamed.
Since the 1970s, many studies, including double-blind trials, have generally failed to find consistent reactions at normal food amounts.
Food Standards Australia New Zealand considers MSG safe for the general population.
In Australia it appears on labels by name or as flavour enhancer 621, and 'no added MSG' products may still contain natural glutamate.
This is general information, so speak with a doctor about any concerns.
Cooking with umami.
Today MSG is mostly made by fermentation.
Bacteria feed on sugars from crops such as sugarcane, corn or cassava and produce glutamate, which is purified and crystallised.
It looks like fine white salt, tastes mild on its own, and lifts soups, stir-fries, stews and dressings.
MSG has roughly a third as much sodium as table salt, so swapping some salt for a little MSG can reduce sodium without losing flavour.
You do not need the crystals to cook with umami.
A splash of soy or fish sauce, a spoonful of tomato paste, a grating of parmesan, a few dried mushrooms or a dab of Vegemite in gravy all deepen flavour in the same way.
The key idea: In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda identified a savoury taste he named umami, then created MSG.
Part two. Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature.
A few degrees can turn silky meat into shoe leather.
Understanding exactly what heat does to proteins explains sous vide, perfect eggs and why chefs swear by thermometers.
Cooking is protein chemistry.
Proteins are long chains folded into specific shapes.
Heat makes them vibrate until the weak bonds holding their shape give way.
They unfold, denaturation, then tangle with their neighbours, coagulation.
That is what turns runny egg white solid and translucent prawn flesh firm and opaque.
The crucial detail is that different proteins set at different temperatures.
In an egg, ovotransferrin starts setting near 62 degrees, the yolk thickens around 65, and ovalbumin needs close to 80.
Hold an egg at 63 to 65 degrees for about an hour and you get a custard-like yolk and a barely set white, as in Japanese onsen tamago, cooked in hot springs.
Boiling water at 100 degrees overshoots everything.
What happens inside meat.
Meat is mostly water held inside muscle proteins and wrapped in connective tissue made largely of collagen.
The muscle protein myosin begins to set at around 50 degrees, so the meat firms but stays juicy.
That is roughly the rare range.
Through the 60s, other proteins, including actin at about 66 degrees or above, contract and squeeze out moisture, and the meat turns noticeably drier.
Collagen behaves differently.
It shrinks at around 60 degrees, but given enough time at higher temperatures it slowly breaks down into gelatine.
That gives braised meat its silky, falling-apart texture.
Hence the cook's dilemma: tender cuts want low temperatures, while tough, collagen-rich cuts need long cooking.
Why sous vide works.
Sous vide is French for 'under vacuum'.
Food is sealed in a bag and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature.
Its culinary use is usually traced to 1974, when chef Georges Pralus used it for foie gras, which lost far less fat under gentle heat.
Food scientist Bruno Goussault later trained chefs in it.
Home circulators became affordable in the 2010s.
Water carries heat much faster than air, which is why you can briefly put a hand in a 200 degree oven but not in boiling water.
Set the bath to 56 degrees for medium-rare steak and the food can never get hotter.
It cooks evenly from edge to centre, with no grey band.
Cooks then add a quick, hot sear for browning.
Time as well as temperature.
Food safety guidance usually gives one number, such as cooking poultry until the centre reaches 75 degrees, which kills bacteria like Salmonella almost instantly.
But bacterial death really depends on temperature and time together.
At lower temperatures bacteria still die, just more slowly.
Food scientists have published tables showing that holding food at a lower temperature for long enough achieves the same reduction as a brief moment at a higher one.
That is how sous vide cooks can safely serve juicier chicken.
These methods need accurate equipment, correct holding times and an understanding of the science.
For everyday home cooking, follow the official temperature guidance and check with a probe thermometer.
The risks and the thermometer.
Precise low temperature cooking has risks that conventional cooking avoids.
In a sealed, airless bag, bacteria that thrive without oxygen, such as Clostridium botulinum, can become a hazard if food is held too long at too low a temperature or cooled slowly afterwards.
Cooking below about 55 degrees for long periods is particularly risky.
Eat cooked food promptly, or chill it quickly in iced water and refrigerate it.
Pregnant people, young children, older adults and those with weakened immunity are generally advised to avoid lightly cooked meat, fish and eggs.
For any cook, the best tool is a probe thermometer.
Once you know the internal temperature, you are no longer guessing, and dry chicken and overcooked steak become far rarer.
The key idea: Heat changes the shape of proteins, and each protein sets at its own temperature, often only a few degrees apart.
Part three. Why chillies burn: the science of heat.
Chilli heat is not a taste at all.
It is a clever chemical trick that fools your pain sensors, and the story of how it conquered the world's kitchens is just as surprising.
From Mexico to the world.
Thai, Indian, Sichuan and Korean food all learned to use chillies only in the last five centuries.
Chillies, plants of the genus Capsicum, originated in the Americas and were domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago.
After Columbus's voyages, Spanish and especially Portuguese traders carried them around the world.
Unlike many crops, they were easy to grow from seed, thrived in warm climates and offered a cheap, intense flavour.
Within about a century they grew in India, Africa and South-East Asia, where local cooks made them their own, often replacing or supplementing black pepper.
How capsaicin fools you.
The burn comes mainly from capsaicinoids, chiefly capsaicin.
Taste buds do not detect it.
Instead it binds to TRPV1, a protein on pain-sensing nerve endings.
TRPV1 normally detects dangerous heat, switching on above roughly 43 degrees Celsius.
Capsaicin flips the same switch, so your brain concludes your mouth is burning though the temperature has not changed.
That is why chilli can make you sweat and flush.
Work on how such receptors sense temperature and pain earned David Julius a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
In 1912 pharmacist Wilbur Scoville measured heat by diluting extract until tasters felt none.
Labs now measure capsaicinoids directly and convert to Scoville units.
A bell pepper scores zero, a jalapeno a few thousand, and the hottest bred varieties exceed two million.
Why plants burn us.
Why would a plant make something that burns?
One explanation is directed deterrence.
Mammals chewing chillies crush the seeds, while birds swallow them whole and spread them in droppings.
Birds' TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin, so they eat the hottest chillies in comfort.
Capsaicin may also protect fruit from fungi: wild chillies in wetter parts of Bolivia, where fungal attack is more common, tend to be hotter.
Scientists still debate how much each factor matters.
Humans are among very few animals that seek out the burn.
Psychologist Paul Rozin calls it benign masochism, like enjoying a roller coaster while your brain knows you are safe.
Endorphins may add pleasure, though how much is uncertain.
Tolerance builds, since repeated exposure makes nerve endings less responsive for a while.
Where the heat hides.
Many people think the seeds are the hottest part.
In fact capsaicin is made mostly in the pale, spongy ribs, or placenta, that hold the seeds.
Seeds taste hot because they press against it.
Removing the ribs and seeds tames a chilli considerably.
Capsaicin is oily.
It dissolves poorly in water but well in fats and alcohol, so gulping water mostly spreads it around.
Dairy such as milk and yoghurt helps, probably because its fat and a protein called casein help carry capsaicin away.
Starchy foods like rice or bread can also give some relief by mopping up the oil.
Handle very hot chillies with gloves, avoid touching your eyes, and take extreme chilli challenges cautiously.
Capsaicin is also the active ingredient in some pain-relief creams and in pepper spray.
Other kinds of fire.
Not every pungent spice works like chilli.
Black pepper gets its bite from piperine, which also activates TRPV1 and a related receptor, though more mildly.
Wasabi, horseradish and mustard rely on isothiocyanates, which are volatile, so the heat rushes up the nose and fades quickly.
They activate a different receptor, TRPA1, which also responds to irritants such as the fumes from cut onions.
Sichuan pepper, from the dried husks of a prickly ash shrub unrelated to chillies or black pepper, does something stranger.
A compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool produces a tingling, buzzing numbness that researchers have compared to a mild vibration on the lips.
Sichuan cooking pairs this numbing sensation with chilli heat in mala, meaning 'numbing and spicy'.
The key idea: Chillies are American plants that spread around the globe within a century of Columbus's voyages.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Kikunae Ikeda's discovery show about savoury taste?
Answer. It is a distinct taste linked to glutamate.
Question two. Why does an egg held at about 64 degrees have a custardy yolk and a soft white?
Answer. Each protein sets at its own temperature.
Question three. Why did chillies spread so quickly after 1492?
Answer. They were easy to grow and full of flavour.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
